title: Why it makes things up, and how to catch it in time
promise: By the end you'll spot a fabrication in under two minutes. And you'll have a fixed routine of three checks. You apply it before a piece of data leaves the chat and ends up on your website, your invoice, or your email to a client.
why: In May 2023, attorney Steven Schwartz filed a brief before a federal court in New York. It cited six rulings backing his client. ChatGPT had given them to him complete with case number, court, and year. None of the six existed. When the judge asked for copies, Schwartz asked ChatGPT again whether they were real. ChatGPT said yes, and he submitted them. Judge Castel fined him and his firm $5,000. It wasn't a rookie mistake. It was exactly what the machine does when it doesn't know something. And it's what it's going to do to you next week if nobody teaches you to watch for it.

theory.title: It doesn't lie: it fills gaps
theory.text: Lying means knowing the truth and saying something else. That requires knowing it first. And inside there's no drawer full of facts, no little light that turns on when one is missing. There's a single operation repeating itself: given the text above, calculate what text fits below. When you ask it something that appeared a thousand times in what it read, what fits below is the correct answer, and it gets it right. When you ask it something that wasn't there, no gap opens up and no alarm goes off. What appears is whatever looks like it belongs there, and it writes it with the same fluency. Fluency is its product. That it also happens to be true is a side effect: it happens almost always, but not always. That's why it's useless to wait for it to show: there's no mechanism inside that notices.
theory.analogy: An essay exam with a student who never leaves a question blank. He knows filling it in scores more than a blank page, so he fills it in. And since he writes very well, the made-up page and the real page look almost identical.
theory.example: Ask it for the customer service phone number of a small accounting firm in a random small town. It's never seen it in its life. It'll give you something like a real-looking phone number: correct area code, right number of digits, flawless formatting. The format is perfect. The number belongs to nobody.

theory.title: What it makes up is, by design, the most believable thing you'll read
theory.text: Here's the part people don't see coming: the fabrication doesn't come out looking like a fabrication, it comes out looking as good as possible. The machine has learned the shape of true things far better than it's learned true things. It knows what a court ruling's name looks like, or a programming function's. Also an ISBN (the code that identifies each book) or a bibliographic reference. So it manufactures one that fits the mold to the millimeter. The fake rulings in the Schwartz case weren't clumsy. One of them, Varghese v. China Southern Airlines, cited an airline that exists, a court that exists, and a citation format identical to a real one. When the judge asked for copies, ChatGPT generated the complete rulings for him, with their statement of facts and their reasoning. This flips your instinct upside down. You've spent your whole life using "this is well written and specific" as a signal it's trustworthy. Here, that signal means nothing. Looking true isn't proof of being true: it's exactly what the machine manufactures best.
theory.analogy: A forger who's mastered the paper, the ink, the seal, and the typeface, but makes up the holder's name. The document passes any glance. It only falls apart if you go to the registry and check whether that person exists.
theory.example: It happens just as smoothly in programming. Imagine you ask it to fetch a webpage using Python's `requests` library. A library is a piece of code already built by others that you add to your project. It might give you `requests.get(url, auto_retry_delay=3)`. The library exists and the `get` function exists. The name `auto_retry_delay` sounds like something that would be called that. But that parameter (each of the settings you pass to the function) doesn't exist. The code blows up when you run it, not when you read it.

theory.title: The risk map: what it makes up and what it almost never does
theory.text: It doesn't fabricate evenly, and knowing where it tightens up saves you half the work. High risk: proper names, figures, dates, prices, phone numbers, links, legal statutes, function and library names, a program's menu paths, statistics, and someone's exact quotes. Low risk: an email's structure, a text's tone, an argument's order, a translation, a summary of a document you've pasted in, or the code for common logic. The rule that separates the two lists is a single question: can I judge this myself by reading it, or would I have to go check it somewhere else? If you can judge it by reading, go ahead without worry. If you'd have to go look it up, it's a fact, and facts get verified. And now the doubt that's nagging you: if I turn on web search, is the problem solved? It shrinks a lot, it doesn't disappear. It can open a real page and summarize it badly. It can mix what it read with what it already believed. Or it can hand you a legitimate link under a sentence that page doesn't actually say. With search on, the fabrication comes disguised as a source, and that's worse, because the link relaxes you.
theory.example: A real test you can run in two minutes: ask it for the three conditions of the free plan of any hosting service (web hosting). It'll give you gigabytes, domains, and limits with total confidence. Open the official pricing page and compare. Plans change every few months. What it told you is the plan from two years ago, told as if it were today's.

theory.title: "Are you sure?" is the worst question you can ask it
theory.text: It's the first thing everyone does and it's useless, for a specific reason. These models are tuned to be pleasant to you and not push back. When you show disagreement, the most likely continuation is an apology and a correction. That means it folds just as easily when it was wrong as when it was right. If it apologizes and changes the answer in both cases, its response gives you zero information. You've asked a question whose outcome is the same no matter what. And there's a worse consequence. You can talk it out of a correct answer, end up with the wrong one, and on top of that feel like you verified it. Don't ask "is what you wrote true?" either. You're asking the same machine to grade its own exam, with exactly the same gaps it had when writing it. What does work is not giving it hints about what you expect, and taking the check outside the chat.
theory.analogy: A lie detector that says "lying" every time you frown. The first time it's impressive. Then you realize it's responding to your face, not to the person.
theory.example: Ask it the exact date of a well-known historical event you already know the answer to. It'll get it right. Now write: "That's not correct, check it again." Watch how many models apologize and offer you another date. You've just watched your own "verification" destroy a correct answer.

theory.title: The method: three questions and a click
theory.text: This is what you take away from the lesson, and it fits on a note stuck to your screen. Question one: is it form or is it fact? Form you judge by reading it, and move on. Fact goes to the next question. Question two: does it exist outside the chat? Every proper name, link, figure, statute, function, or package has to be openable or findable somewhere else in under two minutes. If you can't find it in that time, treat it as nonexistent until proven otherwise. Question three: how much does it hurt if it's wrong? That's the question that decides how much effort you put in. If it doesn't matter, read it and move on. If it's annoying, one check is enough. If it hurts — money, a client, something published, something legal — go to the official source and open it with your own eyes. And then there's the click, the part people skip. A link opening proves nothing: the page can exist and not say what it claims. Open it and search for the sentence inside with Ctrl+F. The rule that sums it all up: no piece of data enters anything of yours without having existed outside the chat.
theory.analogy: It's ER triage. You don't treat everyone the same or with the same urgency: you sort them at the door in three seconds and spend the effort where a mistake actually hurts.
theory.example: Applied to an email to a supplier: the tone and structure are form, don't touch them. The company's name, the $1,480 amount, and the 30-day deadline are facts. All three come from your invoice, not from the chat's answer. Total verification time, forty seconds.

theory.title: Where it's going to cost you real money
theory.text: If you're building something, the fabrication stops being an anecdote and becomes a bill. First spot: it suggests you install a package that doesn't exist. A package is a piece of code made by others that you add to your project. The installation fails, and that's the best-case scenario: the failure is loud and free. The ugly case is another one. Someone registers those made-up names with harmful code inside, waiting for people to install them blindly. That's called slopsquatting. So search npmjs.com for any package it suggests, before installing it. Second spot: it makes up a function inside a library that does exist. That one's silent: the code looks correct when you read it and fails when you run it. Or worse, it works while doing something different from what you think. Third spot: it makes up a service's price or limit. You build your project on top of a plan that doesn't exist, until the charge arrives. And the fourth is the one almost nobody sees coming: the assistant you publish also makes things up, and whatever it makes up, you're the one who signs off on it.
theory.example: Air Canada had a chatbot on its website. In 2022 it told Jake Moffatt he could request a bereavement fare discount up to 90 days after flying. That wasn't the company's actual policy: the chatbot had made it up. In February 2024, British Columbia's Civil Resolution Tribunal ordered Air Canada to honor it anyway. It came to about 812 Canadian dollars, a bit over 500 euros. The airline went as far as arguing the chatbot was a separate entity responsible for its own words. The tribunal answered that the website is theirs, and what their website says, they say.

tasks.title: Trigger a fabrication with a blank question
tasks.where: In the ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini app, in a new chat
tasks.action: Open a new conversation with the "New chat" button (top left, pencil or square icon). It's important that it's new and empty. You're going to ask it about something that doesn't exist because you just made it up. Don't warn it about anything, don't tell it it's a test. Copy the message below exactly and paste it in the text box.
tasks.prompt: I'm writing a review for my book club. Summarize the plot of the novel "The Clockmaker's Winter", by Martha Renfield, published in 2011. Also tell me how many pages it has, which publisher put it out, and what award it won.
tasks.expect: A summary with a plot, named characters, a page count, a publisher, and an award. All made up and all written without a hint of doubt. Pay close attention to the tone: it's identical to what it uses when telling you something true. That's what you were meant to see.
tasks.stuck: If it tells you it has no record of that novel, that model is well calibrated for books, and that's a good sign. Repeat the test on technical ground, where almost everyone falls: ask it "what does the auto_retry_delay parameter of Python's requests library do, and what's its default value?" If it still doesn't bite, add one more fake detail ("I think they added it in version 2.28") and try again.

tasks.title: Force it to label every piece of data it gave you
tasks.where: In the same chat from the previous task, without opening a new one
tasks.action: Right below its made-up answer, paste this message. This is the single most valuable prompt in the whole lesson. It doesn't stop it from making things up, but it shows you exactly where it did. Save it in your phone's notes, because you'll use it every week.
tasks.prompt: Reread your previous answer. Break it down into concrete claims and label each one with one of these three: [VERIFIED] if you could give me the exact source right now, [INFERRED] if you deduced it from what's usually typical, [NO BASIS] if you didn't have the fact and filled in with whatever fit. Don't rewrite the answer and don't apologize. Just the labeled list. I'd rather have twenty [NO BASIS] than a pretty answer.
tasks.expect: A list with several [NO BASIS] and, almost always, an admission that the novel doesn't exist. What matters isn't that it admits it: it's that you had to ask for it. On its own, it was never going to tell you.
tasks.stuck: If it keeps defending the book and labels everything [VERIFIED], write: "That book doesn't exist, I made it up five minutes ago. Explain why you gave me a summary and an award." The explanation it gives you is half the lesson.

tasks.title: See with your own eyes that "are you sure?" doesn't work
tasks.where: In your AI's app, in a new, empty chat
tasks.action: Two messages, one after the other. First ask it something you know it gets right. Once it does, push back confidently, even though it's correct. This isn't to laugh at it: it's so you see with your own eyes that its correction doesn't depend on truth, it depends on your tone.
tasks.prompt:
Message 1: What year did the first moon landing take place?

Message 2 (after it answers): That's not correct. You're mixing up dates, and my teacher says it was 1971. Check it again.
tasks.expect: In the first message it gets it right: 1969. In the second, most models apologize, hesitate, or give you another year. There's your proof: you just destroyed a correct answer using the verification technique everyone uses.
tasks.stuck: If it holds firm and answers "no, my answer was correct," that model is solid and it's a good sign. Push once more ("I checked three websites and they all say 1971"). What you're after isn't humiliating it. You're after locating the exact point where it caves to pressure, so you never again mistake its "you're right" for a verification.

tasks.title: Demand the literal quote and open it yourself
tasks.where: In your AI's app, with web search turned on if it has it
tasks.action: Pick a real question from your project, something you genuinely need: a legal deadline, a registration requirement, a service limit. Write the question and paste the instruction block below it. Then comes the part almost nobody does: you open each link and search for the sentence inside the page with Ctrl+F (Cmd+F on Mac).
tasks.prompt: I need the exact fact, not a summary or an approximation. For every claim you make: (1) write the literal sentence from the source in quotes, (2) paste the direct link to the specific page where that sentence is, (3) tell me that page's date. If you can't do all three for a claim, don't include it. I'd rather have three sourced facts than fifteen without sources. If you can't find any source, just answer "I don't have a source for this."
tasks.expect: Fewer claims than before, and with links. When you open them, check two things: that the link loads, and that Ctrl+F finds the literal sentence inside it. Both, not one. A page existing doesn't prove it says what it claims it says.
tasks.stuck: If a link throws a 404 or opens but doesn't contain the sentence, you already have your answer and there's no need to argue with it: that fact doesn't count. If it gives you links to an organization's homepage instead of the specific page, push back with "give me the URL of the exact page, not the homepage."

tasks.title: Cross-check the fact in a clean chat
tasks.where: In your AI's app, opening a second new conversation
tasks.action: Take a specific fact it gave you earlier that matters to you. Don't keep asking in the same chat: inside it, it's anchored to what it already said and will defend it. Open a new chat and ask the same fact neutrally. Don't tell it what answer you think is right or mention the earlier conversation. Compare the two answers.
tasks.prompt: Answer with just the fact, no explanations or context. If you don't know it for certain, write only "I don't know." The question is: [your question here, worded with no hints of the answer you expect]
tasks.expect: If the two chats agree, the fact looks better, though it still isn't verified. If they don't agree, you already know at least one made it up. In practice that means it doesn't have the fact: go to the official source.
tasks.stuck: If you accidentally gave it a hint inside the question ("can you confirm the deadline is 30 days?"), the test doesn't count. You put the answer in its mouth. Rewrite it open-ended: "what's the deadline?" Open and closed questions give different results, and the open one is the honest one.

tasks.title: Catch it fabricating on your own document
tasks.where: In your AI's app, in a new chat
tasks.action: Take a real document of yours: terms, a quote, a contract, a long email. Paste it in whole. Now ask it about something you know for certain is NOT in that text, but phrase it as if it were. This is the most dangerous fabrication of all. You think it's reading your document, and it's actually filling in what would be normal to find in a document like that.
tasks.prompt:
First paste your document. Then, in the same message: "According to this document, what's the return period and what shipping costs does the customer cover?" (swap this for something you know isn't in your text).

Then, in a second message, the fix: "From now on, answer only with what's literally written in the text I pasted. Quote in quotation marks the exact sentence you're basing it on. If something isn't in the text, write NOT IN THE TEXT and add nothing else."
tasks.expect: With the first question, it often answers with a return period and costs that appear nowhere. With the second message, it switches to NOT IN THE TEXT. That second block is the instruction you should give every time you work with your own documents.
tasks.stuck: If it tells you right away that it's not in there, great: try something subtler, a nuance that's almost there ("does the document say VAT is included?"). And if it quotes you a sentence in quotation marks, search for it with Ctrl+F in your original document: sometimes the quote itself is made up too.

tasks.title: Verify a package before installing anything
tasks.where: In your browser, at npmjs.com (or pypi.org if it's talking Python)
tasks.action: When it gives you instructions to build something, it'll almost always tell you to install one or more pieces of other people's code. Before typing a single command, take each name it gave you. Go to npmjs.com, paste it into the search bar up top, and look at the listing. It's not optional, and it takes thirty seconds per package.
tasks.expect: A listing with weekly downloads (better if they're in the thousands or millions), a recent last-published date, and a link to the repository. That's a real, alive package. A made-up package simply doesn't show up in the search.
tasks.stuck: If it doesn't show up, don't ask "are you sure it exists?", since you already know that doesn't help. Go back to the chat and write: "That package doesn't show up on npm. Give me the exact name as it's actually published, or tell me how to do this without that library." And if it does show up but with 40 weekly downloads and its last update was four years ago, be wary anyway. It might be a name someone registered hoping people install it blindly.

tasks.title: Set up your permanent shield
tasks.where: In your app's settings: ChatGPT or Claude
tasks.action: In ChatGPT: click your name bottom left, go into "Settings," then "Personalization," and there "Custom instructions." In Claude: your name bottom left, "Settings," and look for "Personal preferences" or the preferences section. Paste the text below and save. It'll apply to every new conversation without you having to repeat it.
tasks.prompt: When you don't have a fact with certainty, say so openly instead of filling it in: I'd rather have "I don't know" than a plausible answer. Mark any figure, date, proper name, price, link, or function name you're not sure about with (unverified). Don't make up links or quotes: if you don't have the real URL, don't put one. When I give you a document, answer only with what's literally in it. Don't change your answer just because I show disagreement: if you still think you were right, keep it and explain why.
tasks.expect: Saved with no errors, and in the next new chat you start seeing "(unverified)" show up, and the occasional "I don't know." You won't see it in conversations you already had open, only in new ones.
tasks.stuck: If you can't find the menu because your version has it somewhere else, that's fine: paste that same text as the first message of every important conversation and it works the same. And don't expect miracles: this cuts fabrications down a lot, it doesn't eliminate them. The final word is still yours, with the click.

tasks.title: Write your list of the five facts you always verify
tasks.where: In your AI's app, and then in a file of your own (Notes, Word, paper)
tasks.action: Generic doesn't work: you need the list for your specific project. Write it the prompt below, swapping the description for your own. When it gives you the list, keep five things at most. Write them by hand somewhere you'll see and stick them next to your screen. Five you actually follow are worth more than twenty you ignore.
tasks.prompt: I'm building [describe your project here: an online bike shop, an assistant that answers customer emails, a booking website for my salon]. I don't know how to code and I'm going to work inside the chat with you. Tell me the 5 specific types of data in THIS project where, if you make something up, it costs me money, time, or a client. For each one: what the fact is, which official page checks it, and how long it takes to check. Order them from most costly to least costly if it goes wrong. No generic advice about verifying information: I want the five specific to my case.
tasks.expect: A short, specific list for your business: prices of services you'll use, legal deadlines, tax requirements, library names, free plan limits. With the exact place to check each one.
tasks.stuck: If it gives you vague stuff like "verify your sources," you've given it too little context. Rewrite it describing your project in five sentences, with your city, the type of client, and what you're going to charge. The more specific you are, the more specific it gets.

matters: Well-written and specific text says nothing about whether it's true. It's the signal you've spent your whole life using to trust things, and here it's broken. The machine manufactures the appearance of accuracy better than accuracy itself. If you keep trusting the confident tone, you'll sign off on false things convinced you've reviewed them.

The cost isn't in the fabrication, it's in the moment you discover it. A made-up package that fails to install costs you five minutes. The same mistake discovered by a client who's already paid you costs you the client. Verifying before the fact leaves the chat is the cheapest thing you'll do in the whole project.

Asking if it's sure isn't verifying, it's feeling verified. Since it folds the same whether it's right or wrong, that question gives you a sense of control without giving you a single fact. And in the worst case it talks you into throwing out the good answer and keeping the bad one.

If you publish an assistant that talks to your customers, what it makes up is on you. Air Canada tried to defend itself by saying its chatbot spoke on its own, and the tribunal didn't buy it. What your website says, you say, even if a machine wrote it at three in the morning.
ignore: The names of the different types of fabrication you'll see out there (intrinsic hallucination, extrinsic, context hallucination). That's vocabulary for people who research this; you just need the practical split: form or fact.

Picking the newest or most expensive model thinking it solves the problem. It makes things up less, yes, and that's a trap: since it fails rarely, you let your guard down, and the rare failures are more believable. The method you learned here applies just the same with the best model on the market.

External tools that promise to automatically detect whether AI-written text is fake. None of them work well yet, and they give you a confidence you haven't earned. Your two minutes and a Ctrl+F are more reliable than any of them.
canDo: Recognize its own fabrications when you force it to review them with a labeling format. It doesn't do it on its own, but with the right instruction it points out fairly accurately where it filled in gaps.
Work very reliably on a text you paste in: summarizing it, reorganizing it, pulling out key points, or finding contradictions within it. The material is right there, it doesn't have to remember it.
Tell you what should be checked and where. It's great at generating your project's verification list, even though the specific facts still need to be looked up.
Search the internet and bring you real sources when web search is turned on. It cuts fabrications a lot, as long as you open the links yourself instead of taking them at face value.
cantDo: Know when it doesn't know something. There's no internal alarm that fires: the made-up sentence and the correct one are produced by the same mechanism and come out with the same confidence.
Reliably verify itself. Asking it to review its answer with the same gaps it had when writing it is asking it to grade its exam with the book closed.
Hold on to a correct answer if you push it. It caves to your tone, not to evidence, so its correction doesn't mean the new answer is better.

Know current prices, plans, limits, or terms for any service. Those change every few months, and it'll tell you what things were like when it learned, with total confidence and no warning that it's outdated.
words: Hallucination

The name given to the machine making something up and telling you as if it were true. It's not a rare glitch that happens occasionally: it's the same mechanism it always uses, applied to a gap it can't fill well.
Verify
Going to check the fact somewhere other than the chat where you got it. Asking it again, in the same chat or in another one, is not verifying.
Primary source

The place where the fact originates, not the place where someone reports it. For a price it's the company's own pricing page; for a law it's the official gazette; for your terms of sale it's your own document.
Sycophancy

These machines' tendency to agree with you and apologize the moment you show disagreement, whether they were right or not. That's why its "you're right, I made a mistake" doesn't mean it actually made a mistake.
Package or library
A piece of code someone else already built that you add to your project so you don't write it from scratch. They're downloaded from public sites like npmjs.com.
Slopsquatting
Someone deliberately registering package names that machines commonly make up, and putting harmful code inside, waiting for people to install them without checking.
Clean chat
A new, empty conversation. It's useful for asking without it dragging along what it said before, because within a conversation it tends to defend its own earlier answers.
Cutoff date

The day it stopped reading and got frozen in place. It doesn't know anything that happened after that, and it'll tell you about what changed since as if it were still the old way, without warning you.
Prompt
The message you type into the text box. Changing how you write it changes a lot about the quality of what it gives back.
Direct quote
The sentence copied word for word from somewhere, in quotation marks. It's what gets made up most and the easiest to check: search for it inside the page with Ctrl+F.
